cover.headline: Volumes are back, pricing power is not: a great franchise in a permanently tougher market, now priced about right
cover.lead: Asian Paints is India's largest paint company, with ~1.7 lakh retail touchpoints and 27 plants. Since Grasim launched Birla Opus in Feb-2024 (now the #3 player, Q1FY27 paint revenue ₹1,661 cr, +64%) and JSW bought Akzo Nobel India, it has lost share (59% to 52% of branded decorative paints in the year to Mar-2025, Elara) and pricing power: value growth trailed volume by 4-7 points for two years. Volumes recovered to +8.7% in FY26 and +9.0% in Q1FY27, and price rises to offset the 2026 input spike lifted Q1FY27 revenue 18% and EBITDA 34%, helped by low-cost inventory that management says has now run out. The street values Asian Paints on **P/E (46.5-52x FY28E EPS)**. We forecast EPS of ₹54.6 in FY27E and ₹60.6 in FY28E, in line with the street. Applying **43x to Sep-28E EPS of ₹63.6** gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with HOLD.** Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹2,330, DCF ₹1,386. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: Decorative volume growth recovered from −0.5% (Q2FY25) to 10.9%, 7.9%, 12.4% and 9.0% in the last four quarters; FY27 guidance is 8-10%. In the 2026 supply shock large players gained from small ones. Industrial JVs and international (+27% in Q1FY27) add growth.

arguments.h: Pricing power has been lost, for now
arguments.p: FY26 value growth was only 4.3% on 8.7% volume: price cuts, rebates and down-trading. Discounting has seen "no let-up" (MD, May-2026) and competition is "at an all-time high" (Jul-2026). Birla Opus gained another ~30 bp of share in Q1FY27 alone. Q1FY27's value growth (+16.6%) is price pass-through, not regained pricing power.

arguments.h: Margins: inside the band, not back to FY24
arguments.p: Consolidated EBITDA margin: 21.4% (FY24), 17.7% (FY25), 18.8% (FY26), 20.6% in Q1FY27 on cheap inventory; ~25% input inflation hits Q2. We model {{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.1|pct}} / {{F.ebitdaMargin.2|pct}}, inside the 18-20% guidance. VAM-VAE (from Aug-2026) helps from FY28.

At ₹2,403 the stock trades at 44.0x our FY27E and 39.6x FY28E EPS, against a 59.6x median forward P/E since 2021. After the sector's ~28% de-rating our 43x gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}, just short of a BUY. A DCF at an 11.3% cost of equity gives only ₹1,386: the price still assumes decades of growth.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): how much margin the high-cost inventory takes, and whether volumes hold in the 8-10% band through the festive season.
Raw materials: crude-linked inputs eased from June while TiO2 started rising; management has flagged possible price cuts in H2FY27, which would slow FY28 revenue.
Competition: Birla Opus share gains (Grasim reports quarterly), JSW Dulux's strategy after the Akzo deal, and whether dealer discounting finally eases.
VAM-VAE ramp-up at Dahej (first phase from Aug-2026, 2-2.5 years to approach 150,000 t): the 300-500 bp gross-margin benefit on products using in-house emulsion.
CCI investigation into alleged abuse of dominance (ordered Jul-2025): a finding against the company would bring a penalty and curbs on dealer practices.

sections.title: India's paint leader, plus kitchens, bath, lighting, industrial JVs and 13 countries abroad

blocks.p: Asian Paints makes and sells paint. Most of it is **decorative paint for homes in India**: interior and exterior emulsions (Royale, Apex, Apcolite, Tractor, Ace), enamels, wood finishes, wall putty, waterproofing (SmartCare, Damp Proof) and adhesives, sold through ~1.7 lakh retail touchpoints that tint colours to order. This sits in the listed company (the "standalone" entity, ₹30,769 cr of revenue in FY26, 86% of the group), together with kitchens (Sleek, ₹400 cr) and bath fittings (Ess Ess, ₹347 cr). The rest (₹4,815 cr after eliminations) comes from subsidiaries: **international** paint operations in South Asia, the Middle East, Africa and the South Pacific (₹3,340 cr), **industrial coatings** through Asian Paints PPG (protective and powder coatings, ₹1,334 cr) and small **home-decor** businesses (White Teak lighting, Weatherseal windows). A second PPG venture, PPG Asian Paints (car and industrial coatings, ₹2,468 cr), is an associate: only Asian Paints' half of its profit is counted.

sections.title: A growing market that turned from a cosy oligopoly into a price war

blocks.p: India's decorative paint market grows with new homes, repainting and the shift from lime wash and unorganised brands to branded emulsions. For decades it was a stable oligopoly: Asian Paints, Berger, Kansai Nerolac and Akzo Nobel (Dulux) together held most of the branded market, raised prices together and earned high returns. That changed in 2024. Grasim launched Birla Opus with ~₹10,000 cr of planned investment (Grasim) and a large capacity build-out, and in 2025 JSW Paints bought control of Akzo Nobel India (now JSW Dulux). New entrants pay dealers more, give contractors bigger schemes and discount the economy range hardest.

The cost side is a petrochemical cycle with one big exception: titanium dioxide (TiO2), the white pigment, is the largest single input and is not linked to crude. Monomers, solvents and emulsions are. The West Asia conflict from early 2026 pushed material costs up ~20-25%; the industry raised prices ~13-14% in steps between March and June. Material is only ~35-40% of what a household pays per square foot (labour is the rest), which is why demand has absorbed price rises so far.

Grasim's Birla Opus (launched Feb-2024) was the #3 organised decorative player by Q1FY27 with revenue of Rs1,661 cr (+64% YoY) and 1,450+ franchise outlets; its share rose ~30 bp QoQ and, with Birla White putty, is 'nearing early teens' (Grasim, Aug-2026). JSW Paints took control of Akzo Nobel India (now JSW Dulux) in 2025. Asian Paints says discounting has seen 'no let-up' and intensity is 'at an all-time high'.

Elara (via Reuters): Asian Paints' share of branded decorative paints fell from 59% to 52% in the twelve months to Mar-2025; Systematix (via Outlook Business): 53% (FY23) to 47% (FY25). FY26-Q1FY27 volume growth of 9-12% suggests the loss has slowed; management says it grew 'slightly higher than the industry' in Q1FY27. No audited share data exist.

For two years value growth trailed volume by 4-7 points (price cuts, down-trading to putty and economy emulsions, higher rebates). In Q1FY27 value (+16.6%) ran ahead of volume (+9%) because of price increases. Management expects value > volume 'till the time we get into pricing corrections'.

Material inflation ~20-25% from Mar-2026 against ~11% price increases by May and ~13-14% by June; Q1FY27 margins were protected by low-cost inventory, Q2 carries the higher cost. TiO2 (largest input, not crude-linked) started rising at end-June while monomers eased.
Rural and T3/T4 towns ahead of large cities; B2B (factories, government, hospitality projects) strong. Management guides 8-10% FY27 decorative volume growth.

VAM-VAE (Dahej, ~Rs3,250 cr) starting Aug-2026: 300-500 bp gross-margin benefit on products using in-house emulsion, ramping over 2-2.5 years; white cement (Fujairah) operational. Rivals buy these inputs.
CCI DG investigation (ordered 1-Jul-2025) into alleged abuse of dominance on Grasim's complaint; penalties under the Competition Act can go up to 10% of turnover.

sections.title: New competition: share lost, pricing power dented, margins reset lower

blocks.p: This is the question that decides the stock. Since Feb-2024 Asian Paints has faced two new competitors with deep pockets. **Birla Opus** (Grasim) reached the #3 position in organised decorative paints within about two years; its Q1FY27 paint revenue was ₹1,661 cr, up 64%, with 1,450+ franchise outlets, and its revenue share rose another ~30 bp in the quarter (Grasim). **JSW Dulux** (JSW Paints after buying 74.76% of Akzo Nobel India for ~₹8,986 cr) is the other; its consolidated revenue fell 3% in Q1FY27 (Screener). Asian Paints sold its own 4.42% stake in Akzo India for ~₹734 cr in Jul-2025.

bullets: **Where the fight is.** Management says discounting is most intense in the economy range (putty, low-end emulsions), where "you can really convert a contractor much better if you were to do higher discounting". Asian Paints has chosen to defend volume there, which is why its mix was negative for two years.

**What has gone right.** Volume growth is back to 8-12%; in the 2026 supply shock medium and large players took share from small ones; premium and luxury ranges and new products (17% of revenue) are growing; B2B projects and industrial coatings are strong.

**What the bulls say.** Nomura upgraded in May-2026 arguing Birla Opus is shifting from chasing share to profitability and the price war may have peaked; Elara thinks significant share loss "may be in the past". Grasim's Q1FY27 commentary still talks of "sustaining market share gains".

**Regulation.** The CCI ordered a DG investigation on 1-Jul-2025 into Grasim's complaint that Asian Paints hindered Birla Opus's entry by pressuring dealers, suppliers and landlords. The company says it has a reasonable defence; the outcome is open.

blocks.callout: **Our verdict:** the share loss is slowing but has not reversed, and pricing power has not come back: Q1FY27's strong value growth is cost pass-through that may partly reverse in H2 if inputs fall. We think margins have reset from the 21-22% of FY21 and FY24 to the 18-20% band for good, and we model 19.0-19.2%. Our 43x target multiple prices a still-dominant but no-longer-unchallenged leader; the street's 50x is closer to the pre-2024 multiple.

bullets: **What it is.** Asian Paints Ltd itself: decorative paints in India (~97% of it), plus kitchens and bath fittings. Revenue ₹30,769 cr in FY26, 86% of the group; it grew only 10.7% a year since FY21 because FY22-23's price-led jump was followed by three flat years.

**Margins track inputs and competition.** Standalone EBITDA margin: FY20 22.4%, FY21 24.3%, FY22 18.2%, FY23 19.3%, FY24 22.6%, FY25 18.8%, FY26 20.1%. FY22 was the last input spike; FY25 was price cuts and competition; FY26 recovered on deflation. Standalone gross margin hit a record 45.6% in Q4FY26.

**Q1FY27.** Revenue +16.7% (volume +9%, value +16.6%: ~7% weighted price plus ~3% better mix); gross margin 43.8% (+66 bp) and EBITDA margin 22% (+259 bp) on low-cost inventory and cost cuts. Material inflation was ~25%.

**Pricing.** ~10.4% cumulative increase by end-May 2026 (Q4FY26 deck) and further rises in June; dealers cite ~13-14% at list level. Management expects ~8-9% pricing benefit in Q2, no further increases unless costs become "alarming", and has flagged possible price changes in H2 if inputs ease.

**Kitchen and bath** (inside standalone): kitchen revenue ₹108 cr in Q1FY27 (+10%), loss near break-even; bath ₹85 cr (−4%), loss ₹9 cr. Together ~₹750 cr a year after more than a decade: not a growth driver.

The risk is not volume; it is that competitors keep discounting while inputs stay high, as in FY22 (18.2%) and FY25 (18.8%).

sections.title: Competitive advantage: still the widest in Indian paints, but no longer unbreachable

verdicts: India's most recognised paint brand; consistent heavy spending (cricket/BCCI, 'Rang De India'); 17% of revenue from products launched in the last three years.
Pricing power at the premium end; weaker in economy products where contractors switch for discounts.
~1.7 lakh retail touchpoints, 6,000+ added in FY26; Birla Opus built 1,450+ franchise outlets and a large dealer base within two years by offering higher dealer margins and schemes.
The network was the moat; it proved replicable with money. Asian Paints still has the deepest reach.
27 plants, 1.85 mn KL capacity; in the 2026 supply shock large players gained share from small ones (management, brokers).
Lowest cost to serve; resilience in shocks.
VAM-VAE (Dahej) and white cement (Fujairah): 300-500 bp gross-margin benefit on products using in-house VAE, ramping over 2-2.5 years.
Unique among Indian paint makers; benefits are a few years out and partly offset by start-up costs.
'World's largest' home-painting service (Beautiful Homes); 9+ lakh painters trained.

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** Asian Paints still has the strongest brand, the deepest dealer and tinting network, the lowest cost to serve and, from FY27, a backward-integration edge nobody else in India has. But the last two years proved that its biggest moat, the dealer network, can be copied by a rival willing to spend: Birla Opus built a national network and reached #3 in about two years by paying dealers and contractors more. The moat now protects **volume and leadership**, not **price**. A franchise that once set prices for the industry now has to match competitors' discounts. That is a narrower moat than the one the 60x-80x multiples of 2021-24 were paying for.

sections.title: Ten years of growth, but EPS barely moved in FY21-26 as competition and input costs bit

blocks.p: Asian Paints' revenue grew from ₹14,271 cr in FY16 to ₹35,584 cr in FY26, about 9.6% a year, and profit attributable to shareholders from ₹1,745 cr to ₹4,325 cr, about 9.5% a year. The last five years were rough. Revenue jumped 34% in FY22 and 19% in FY23 as the company passed on a raw-material spike, then stalled: +3% in FY24, −4.5% in FY25 (price cuts, weak demand and Birla Opus's launch) and +5% in FY26. EPS went from ₹32.7 (FY21) to ₹56.9 (FY24) and back to ₹38.2 (FY25) and ₹45.1 (FY26): only 6.6% a year over FY21-26.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** two forces explain the last five years. First, input costs: paints are made from crude derivatives and titanium dioxide, and every spike (FY22, early 2026) squeezes margins until prices catch up. Second, competition: since Birla Opus launched in Feb-2024 Asian Paints has cut prices, raised dealer schemes and grown value slower than volume. FY24's 21.4% EBITDA margin was earned on cheap inputs before the new entrants arrived; we do not expect it again.

bullets: Volume growth ~9% 'across the months'; rural and T3/T4 towns ahead of T1/T2 cities; B2B projects strong in urban markets.

Weighted price increase ~7% in Q1 (taken in April, May and June); with the mix of increases, the pricing effect should be ~8-9% in Q2. No further increase intended 'unless the situation really becomes alarming'.
Material inflation ~25% in Q1; low-cost finished-goods inventory 'seeped through in 1Q'; Q2 is seasonally lower-margin and will carry the higher-cost inventory.
FY27 guidance kept: decorative volume growth 8-10%; consolidated PBDIT margin 18-20%.
Value growth will stay above volume growth 'till the time we get into pricing corrections'; price changes in H2 'could trigger demand even further' (i.e. cuts are possible if raw materials fall).

Competitive intensity 'seems to be at an all-time high'; discounting most intense in economy products, where contractors can be converted with higher discounts. Medium and large players gained from smaller ones during supply disruptions.

VAM-VAE plant (Dahej): first phase from August 2026; 1,00,000 t VAM and 1,50,000 t VAE; 2-2.5 years to approach 150,000 t; 300-500 bp gross-margin benefit on products that use in-house emulsion. White cement plant in Fujairah (UAE) 'fully operational'.
Industrial JV price increases lag (key accounts); margins down ~120 bp in both JVs; management expects industrial to keep outgrowing decorative.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** management has delivered on volume (8-10% guided, 8.7% in FY26, 9.0% in Q1FY27) and on the 18-20% margin band in FY26. The open question for FY27 is not demand but cost: with material inflation of ~25% against ~8-9% price, Q2 margins fall, and H2 depends on crude and TiO2. Our forecast ({{F.ebitdaMargin.0|pct}} for FY27E) assumes the band holds.

sections.title: Returns halved from the 40s to the mid-20s: more capital, lower margins

blocks.p: Asian Paints used to be one of India's highest-return companies: ROCE of 42% in FY15-16 and 29-38% in FY19-FY24. It was 26% in FY25 and FY26. Two reasons. Margins fell (above). And the company stepped up investment: capex was ₹5,813 cr in FY24-26 against ₹2,286 cr in FY21-23, for new paint capacity, the VAM-VAE emulsion plant at Dahej (~₹3,250 cr committed), a white-cement plant in the UAE and home-decor businesses (White Teak, Weatherseal) that still lose money. Operating cash flow was ₹17,616 cr over FY24-26 (FY26 ₹7,088 cr, helped by a ₹976 cr inventory release) and dividends ₹8,116 cr.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** management has committed ~₹2,000 cr to a new paint plant in Madhya Pradesh, ~₹340 cr to a second UAE plant and the balance of VAM-VAE. We model ₹1,400 cr of capex a year, about 3-3.5% of revenue. The payout policy (60% of profit) is reliable; the risk is more money going into home decor, where returns so far are negative.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean accounts, strong cash, recurring "one-off" impairments

bullets: **Cash backs profit.** Operating cash flow was 164% of attributable profit in FY26 (helped by a ₹976 cr inventory release), 121% in FY25 and 112% in FY24; over FY15-26 cash from operations (₹39,057 cr) exceeded profit (₹35,707 cr). FY22 (33%) was the exception, when inventory was built during the input spike.

**"Exceptional" items keep recurring.** −₹363 cr in FY25 (Ethiopia devaluation, White Teak and Causeway impairments, Indonesia exit) and −₹158 cr in FY26 (White Teak intangibles ₹94 cr, new labour code ₹64 cr). Most of it is the cost of home-decor acquisitions that did not work. We treat them as real costs of capital allocation, not as noise.

**Other income is meaningful.** ₹728 cr in FY26 on Screener's basis (after exceptional items), 12% of pre-tax profit. It includes ₹287 cr of mark-to-market gains on funds, ₹181 cr of interest and ₹166 cr share of PPG Asian Paints' profit.

**Minorities.** Screener's consolidated "Net Profit" is before minorities (₹4,395 cr in FY26) while EPS is after (₹4,325 cr); we use the attributable figure throughout. Minorities (₹42-97 cr a year) are mainly PPG's half of Asian Paints PPG.

**Revenue recognition.** Revenue is net of discounts and schemes; the auditor's key audit matter for the parent is revenue cut-off, the second is goodwill impairment (₹219 cr). Rising dealer schemes reduce reported revenue rather than appear as costs, which is why value growth trailed volume.

**Disclosure.** No segment reporting; decorative revenue and margins are not disclosed. Volume growth is disclosed only as a percentage. Business-line PBT is given for the JVs, international and home decor.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Unqualified audit (Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP; S R B C & Co proposed from the 2026 AGM under mandatory rotation), strong cash conversion and a simple balance sheet. The things to watch are the size of dealer schemes netted from revenue, and further impairments in home decor.

sections.title: Net cash of ~₹6,600 cr; working capital tightened in FY26

blocks.p: Asian Paints is net cash. At Mar-2026 it held ₹1,074 cr of cash, ₹7,062 cr of investments and ₹2,439 cr of term deposits (inside other financial assets), against ₹3,929 cr of borrowings, of which ₹1,636 cr are leases and ₹805 cr long-term debt taken over with the polymers subsidiary that is building VAM-VAE. Net cash was ~₹6,600 cr. Working-capital days fell from 52 to 38 in FY26 as inventory came down from 142 to 118 days; receivables have stayed at ~46 days, above the 30-38 days of FY15-20, a sign of more generous dealer credit in a competitive market.

sections.title: Ownership: three founding families at 52.6%, domestic institutions now 21%

blocks.p: The founding Choksi, Dani and Vakil families and their relatives own 52.63% (Jun-2026) through ~80 family accounts and holding companies. Foreign investors own 13.32%, Indian institutions 20.7% and the public 13.19%. Indian institutions' share doubled from ~11% to ~21% in two years, partly because Reliance sold most of its 4.9% stake (3.64% to SBI Mutual Fund at ₹2,201 a share in Jun-2025, and a further ~85 lakh shares in a later block deal). Shareholders numbered ~9.6 lakh at Jun-2026, down from ~12.1 lakh at Mar-2025.

sections.title: The street: mostly Buy, targets ₹2,720-3,750, set when the stock was ~₹2,760

blocks.p: Ten houses published around the Q1FY27 results (28-31 Jul 2026). Buys: ICICI Securities ₹3,180, Anand Rathi ₹3,180 (upgraded), Axis Securities ₹3,270, MNCL ₹3,165 (initiation) and Nomura ₹3,750 (upgraded to Buy in May). Accumulate: Elara ₹3,100 and Deven Choksey ₹2,970. Neutral/Hold: Motilal Oswal ₹3,050 and Prabhudas Lilladher ₹2,720. JM Financial raised its target to ₹2,930. The median target is ~₹3,165 (average ₹3,149), set when the stock was ~₹2,720-2,760; by 30-Sep-2026 the price had fallen to ₹2,403 with the rest of the paint and consumer sector, so the same targets now imply ~32% upside. Every house that discloses a method uses **P/E on FY28E EPS, at 46.5-52x**. Before the results, a consensus of 35 analysts had an average target of ₹2,848. Bulls focus on volume recovery, backward integration and an end to the price war; bears and neutrals on competition, input costs and valuation.

blocks.callout: **What the cross-checks tell us.** EV/EBITDA (24x Sep-28E EBITDA of ₹8,835 cr plus net cash) gives ₹2,330, ~15% below the P/E target: 24x comes from the 39.9x median trailing EV/EBITDA since 2021, cut by the same sector de-rating and restated for Sep-28E EBITDA being 22% above the twelve months to Jun-26 (₹7,240 cr). Trailing EV/EBITDA history does not carry the FY24-25 earnings distortion that lifts the forward P/E median, so it is the more conservative yardstick. The DCF (₹1,386) is far lower: at an 11.3% cost of equity, 6% terminal growth and margins held near 19%, 15 years of ~8% growth support only ~58% of today's price. Asian Paints has always looked expensive on a DCF; the market pays for the length and safety of its growth. With competition now permanent, that premium deserves to be smaller than it was.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a leader worth owning lower down; HOLD at 39.6x FY28E

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** India's paint leader, with the strongest brand and distribution, volume growth back at 8-12%, a backward-integration cost edge coming, net cash of ~₹6,600 cr, a 21.2% ROE and a reliable 60% payout.

**What you are paying:** 44.0x our FY27E and 39.6x FY28E EPS for ~10% EPS growth after FY27, in an industry where two deep-pocketed rivals are still taking share and margins have reset to 18-20%. On the street's method and our inputs the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): HOLD, close to the BUY line.

head: Term
What it means
rows: Paints for homes and buildings (wall emulsions, enamels, wood finishes, putty, waterproofing), sold through dealers who tint colours to order. Distinct from industrial coatings for cars, factories and machines.
Growth in litres/kilos sold vs growth in rupee sales. Value below volume means lower prices, bigger discounts or a shift to cheaper products (e.g. putty).
Value growth minus volume growth, in percentage points.
The listed company Asian Paints Ltd on its own (mostly decorative paints in India), excluding subsidiaries.
Our second business line: consolidated figures less standalone (international, Asian Paints PPG, home-decor subsidiaries, less inter-company eliminations).
PPG Asian Paints (car and industrial coatings; 50%, equity-accounted) and Asian Paints PPG (protective and powder coatings; 50%, consolidated): joint ventures with PPG Industries of the US.
Decorative paint businesses of Grasim (Aditya Birla group, launched Feb-2024) and of JSW Paints (which bought control of Akzo Nobel India, maker of Dulux, in 2025).
Titanium dioxide (white pigment, the largest raw material); vinyl acetate monomer and vinyl acetate-ethylene emulsion (binders used in paints and adhesives), which Asian Paints now makes at Dahej.
Revenue less raw-material cost, as % of revenue. Company decks use net sales; Screener's version includes traded goods.
Operating profit before depreciation, interest and tax (and here before other income). Asian Paints calls it PBDIT.
The share of subsidiaries' profit owned by partners (e.g. PPG's 50% of Asian Paints PPG); excluded from the profit attributable to Asian Paints' shareholders.

Shares given as security for a loan; if the borrower defaults the lender can sell them.

Discounted cash flow valuation; WACC is the required annual return used to discount future cash (here the cost of equity, as Asian Paints has net cash).
